items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: I need ___ pen to sign this form.
items.explanation: Use 'a' before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound: 'a pen'.

rationales.a: Use 'a' before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound: 'a pen'.
rationales.an: Pen begins with the consonant sound /p/, so use a, not an.
rationales.these: 'These' refers to more than one thing; 'pen' is singular.

findings: The pencil-test frame recurred four times and the feedback did not explain any choice.
audit.microSkill: A before a consonant sound
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects a singular object with its article.
audit.levelReason: A short everyday request tests a basic article.
audit.similarityNote: The only consonant-sound article gap; the later email item tests an.

items.setupText: Choose the number that matches the situation.
items.taskText: One ticket is for me and one is for my husband. I want ___ tickets, please.
items.explanation: One ticket for each of two people makes two tickets.

rationales.three: Three would include one more ticket than the two people need.
rationales.two: One ticket for each of two people makes two tickets.
rationales.four: Four would give the two people two tickets each, not one.
rationales.ten: Ten is a different quantity; only two tickets are requested.

findings: The books-on-desk item used a repeated frame and generic noun-fit feedback.
audit.microSkill: Cardinal number with a plural noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses a simple purchase to connect a number word with a quantity.
audit.levelReason: Only familiar people, tickets and two one-item amounts are involved.
audit.similarityNote: A quantity reading task rather than article selection.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: I cannot pay. I do not have ___ money.
items.explanation: 'Not any money' means no money. 'Any' can go before the uncountable noun 'money'.

rationales.many: 'Many' goes with plural things we count, such as 'coins'; 'money' is uncountable.
rationales.a: We do not say a money for cash; use a coin or a note for one piece.
rationales.any: 'Not any money' means no money. 'Any' can go before the uncountable noun 'money'.
rationales.these: These needs a plural countable noun, such as notes, not money.

findings: The original repeated the money sentence and added an unnecessary after-lunch tail.
audit.microSkill: Any with an uncountable noun after not
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes money from countable coins or notes.
audit.levelReason: A direct negative statement uses familiar shopping language.
audit.similarityNote: Negative quantity with money, distinct from the positive bread request.

items.setupText: Choose the words that match the opening times.
items.taskText: The cafe opens Monday to Sunday. It opens ___.
items.explanation: Every day includes all seven days, matching Monday to Sunday.

rationales.one day a week: That describes one opening day, but the cafe opens on seven days.
rationales.on Mondays only: Only Mondays leaves out Tuesday to Sunday.
rationales.at weekends only: The cafe also opens from Monday to Friday.
rationales.every day: Every day includes all seven days, matching Monday to Sunday.

findings: Each student has a name card was repeated and did not teach the meaning of each.
audit.microSkill: Every in a daily routine
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that every day includes each day of the week.
audit.levelReason: Reading a simple weekly schedule is an A1 practical task.
audit.similarityNote: Frequency meaning rather than singular-noun agreement.

items.setupText: Choose the words for an amount of food, without saying an exact amount.
items.taskText: Please cut ___ for lunch.
items.explanation: Some bread gives an amount without saying how many slices.

rationales.some bread: Some bread gives an amount without saying how many slices.
rationales.two slices of bread: This gives an exact number of slices; the request asks for no exact amount.
rationales.these bread: 'Bread' is not plural here, so 'these' cannot go directly before it.
rationales.many bread: Use 'many slices of bread' when counting slices; 'bread' itself is uncountable.

findings: The water-for-lunch frame was duplicated; the feedback ignored countability and possible drink-serving uses.
audit.microSkill: Some for an unspecified food amount
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts an amount of bread with a counted number of slices.
audit.levelReason: A familiar meal request introduces basic uncountable quantity.
audit.similarityNote: Includes a grammatical but explicitly unsuitable exact-quantity option.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: There is ___ email from the hotel in my inbox.
items.explanation: Use an before the vowel sound at the start of email.

rationales.a: 'Email' starts with a vowel sound, so the article is 'an'.
rationales.an: Use an before the vowel sound at the start of email.
rationales.many: Many emails would need a plural noun and There are.
rationales.those: 'Those emails' is plural, but this sentence has 'is' and singular 'email'.

findings: Changing Mina to Lena left the same pencil-test item and feedback.
audit.microSkill: An before a vowel sound
audit.pedagogicalValue: Relates article choice to the first sound of email.
audit.levelReason: A single incoming message supplies a basic singular-noun context.
audit.similarityNote: Vowel-sound counterpart to the pen item in a different sentence structure.

items.setupText: Choose the word for one thing near the speaker.
items.taskText: Look at ___ photo here in my hand.
items.explanation: This points to one thing near the speaker, such as the photo in their hand.

rationales.these: 'These' is for more than one photo; 'photo' is singular.
rationales.that: That usually points to something farther away; the task asks for the near form.
rationales.this: This points to one thing near the speaker, such as the photo in their hand.
rationales.those: Those is for plural things farther away, not this one nearby photo.

findings: The desk-books sentence differed from 1082 only by its location tail.
audit.microSkill: This for a nearby singular referent
audit.pedagogicalValue: Combines distance and number in demonstrative choice.
audit.levelReason: Here, hand and photo give concrete beginner-level reference.
audit.similarityNote: Singular near reference; the shoes item tests plural near reference.

items.setupText: Choose the word for more than one thing near the speaker.
items.taskText: Are ___ shoes here by my feet yours?
items.explanation: These points to plural things near the speaker, here the shoes by their feet.

rationales.this: 'This' goes with one thing; 'shoes' is plural.
rationales.that: That is singular and does not match shoes.
rationales.those: 'Those' is the farther-away form; the task asks for the near form.
rationales.these: These points to plural things near the speaker, here the shoes by their feet.

findings: The repeated money sentence gained only the tail at home; the wrong feedback remained generic.
audit.microSkill: These for nearby plural objects
audit.pedagogicalValue: Links these to plural objects in a question.
audit.levelReason: A simple possession question uses visible everyday objects.
audit.similarityNote: Plural near reference in a question rather than the photo imperative.

items.setupText: Choose the word for one thing far from the speaker.
items.taskText: ___ building over there is our hotel.
items.explanation: That points to one thing farther away, matching building over there.

rationales.That: That points to one thing farther away, matching building over there.
rationales.This: This is the near form; the task asks for a distant building.
rationales.These: 'These' refers to several nearby things; 'building' is singular.
rationales.Those: 'Those' is the distant plural form, but only one building is named.

findings: The name-card item repeated 1084 with only on Monday added.
audit.microSkill: That for a distant singular object
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses over there as a clear distance cue.
audit.levelReason: A short statement identifies a familiar place.
audit.similarityNote: Singular distant reference, completing a different demonstrative contrast.

items.setupText: Choose the word for several things far from the speaker.
items.taskText: Can you read ___ signs over there, across the road?
items.explanation: Those matches the plural signs and the distance across the road.

rationales.that: 'That' needs a singular noun such as 'sign'.
rationales.those: Those matches the plural signs and the distance across the road.
rationales.this: This is singular and near; neither matches the task.
rationales.these: 'These' is plural but points to nearby things; the signs are distant.

findings: The water item repeated an existing frame with an in-the-kitchen tail.
audit.microSkill: Those for distant plural objects
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates plural number from distance when choosing a demonstrative.
audit.levelReason: A short question uses concrete signs and a road.
audit.similarityNote: Plural distant reference in a can-you question.

items.setupText: Choose the form used before a noun in modern standard written English.
items.taskText: I live here. This is ___ address.
items.explanation: 'My' goes before a noun to show that it belongs or relates to the speaker.

rationales.mine: Mine can stand alone, as in The address is mine; it does not go before address.
rationales.me: 'Me' is an object form, not a word showing whose address it is.
rationales.my: 'My' goes before a noun to show that it belongs or relates to the speaker.
rationales.I: 'I' is used as a subject, as in 'I live here', not before 'address'.

findings: Hana replaced another name in the same pencil sentence; no new decision was added.
audit.microSkill: My before a noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts the possessive determiner my with mine, me and I.
audit.levelReason: Personal information and first-person forms are beginner foundations.
audit.similarityNote: First-person ownership in an address statement.

items.setupText: Choose the form used before a noun in standard written English.
items.taskText: Sara cannot find ___ phone.
items.explanation: Her goes before phone to show that the phone belongs to Sara.

rationales.hers: 'Hers' replaces a noun phrase, but 'phone' is still present.
rationales.she: 'She' is a subject form; use 'her' to show whose phone it is.
rationales.herself: Herself refers back to Sara as a person; it does not introduce phone.
rationales.her: Her goes before phone to show that the phone belongs to Sara.

findings: The books-on-desk item added by the window but retained the same easy choices.
audit.microSkill: Her as a possessive determiner
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes possessive her from subject and standalone forms.
audit.levelReason: A missing phone provides a common, short personal situation.
audit.similarityNote: Third-person possession in a negative ability statement.

items.setupText: Choose the possessive form used in standard written English.
items.taskText: We start work at nine. ___ first break is at eleven.
items.explanation: Our goes before first break and shows that the break is for us.

rationales.Our: Our goes before first break and shows that the break is for us.
rationales.Ours: Ours stands alone; it cannot introduce first break.
rationales.Us: 'Us' is an object form, as in 'Tell us', not a possessive word before 'break'.
rationales.We: 'We' is a subject pronoun; 'Our first break' is the subject needed here.

findings: The money item repeated the same negative sentence with before dinner appended.
audit.microSkill: Our before an adjective and noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows that a possessive determiner can come before first plus a noun.
audit.levelReason: Work and break times are accessible daily-routine language.
audit.similarityNote: Plural possessors and an intervening adjective distinguish this possession item.

items.setupText: Choose the word that points back to the same bag.
items.taskText: I bought a bag yesterday. ___ bag is blue.
items.explanation: The bag points back to the bag already introduced with a bag.

rationales.A: A bag would introduce a bag without clearly pointing back to the one just mentioned.
rationales.The: The bag points back to the bag already introduced with a bag.
rationales.An: Bag begins with a consonant sound, so an bag is incorrect.
rationales.Some: Some bag does not clearly identify the previously mentioned bag; use the for that reference.

findings: The name-card sentence was duplicated with an unrelated park setting.
audit.microSkill: The for a previously mentioned object
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows the common a-to-the pattern across two sentences.
audit.levelReason: Only a basic purchase and a color need to be understood.
audit.similarityNote: Backward reference across sentences, not a sound-based article choice.

items.setupText: Choose the word that means zero.
items.taskText: My key box is empty. There are ___ keys in it.
items.explanation: 'No keys' means zero keys, which matches an empty box.

rationales.some: 'Some keys' would mean that the box is not empty.
rationales.two: Two keys would be a positive number; the box has none.
rationales.no: 'No keys' means zero keys, which matches an empty box.
rationales.many: 'Many keys' means a large number, not an empty box.

findings: The repeated water-for-lunch sentence had an unhelpful on-the-bus tail.
audit.microSkill: No before a plural noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Expresses zero directly without adding not.
audit.levelReason: An empty box gives a concrete cue for basic quantity.
audit.similarityNote: Positive sentence form with negative quantity, unlike not any money.

items.setupText: Choose the word that includes the two shops.
items.taskText: The bread shop is open and the fruit shop is open. ___ shops are open.
items.explanation: Both means the two together: the bread shop and the fruit shop.

rationales.One: 'One' needs singular 'shop' and does not include the two shops.
rationales.No: No shops are open would mean the two shops are closed.
rationales.Every: 'Every' takes a singular noun: 'every shop'. It cannot go before 'shops'.
rationales.Both: Both means the two together: the bread shop and the fruit shop.

findings: Luis was another name substitution in the pencil-test frame.
audit.microSkill: Both for a pair
audit.pedagogicalValue: Links both with two named places and a plural noun.
audit.levelReason: Two short opening-status statements make the quantity explicit.
audit.similarityNote: Introduces pair inclusion without the either/neither contrasts reserved for later bands.

items.setupText: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: This road is busy. There are ___ buses.
items.explanation: 'A lot of buses' means a large number of buses; keep 'of' before the noun.

rationales.a lot of: 'A lot of buses' means a large number of buses; keep 'of' before the noun.
rationales.a lot: 'A lot' needs 'of' when a noun follows: 'a lot of buses'.
rationales.much: 'Much' goes with uncountable nouns; 'buses' are countable and plural.
rationales.many of: 'Many of' needs a word such as 'the' before 'buses': 'many of the buses'.

findings: The repeated desk-books sentence ended with the awkward with the teacher.
audit.microSkill: A lot of before a noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Teaches the complete quantity phrase and distinguishes it from many of.
audit.levelReason: A busy road supports a common beginner quantity expression.
audit.similarityNote: Multiword quantity expression rather than a single determiner.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question.
items.taskText: How ___ emails did you send today?
items.explanation: How many asks for the number of plural countable things, here emails.

rationales.much: 'Much' asks about an uncountable amount; individual emails can be counted.
rationales.many: How many asks for the number of plural countable things, here emails.
rationales.some: How some does not form a question about a number.
rationales.any: How any is not the quantity-question pattern; use how many emails.

findings: The negative-money item repeated earlier material and added before the bell.
audit.microSkill: How many with plural count nouns
audit.pedagogicalValue: Asks for a number using a countable plural noun.
audit.levelReason: A short past-tense question has a familiar communication context.
audit.similarityNote: Count question, contrasted with the next item's uncountable cost question.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical question.
items.taskText: How ___ rent do you pay each month?
items.explanation: 'How much' asks for an amount; 'rent' here is an amount of money.

rationales.many: 'Rent' is an amount of money here, not plural things to count.
rationales.a: How a rent is not a question about an amount.
rationales.much: 'How much' asks for an amount; 'rent' here is an amount of money.
rationales.every: 'Every' refers to all members of a group and cannot follow 'how' in this amount question.

findings: The name-card sentence repeated the same singular-noun contrast with a lesson tail.
audit.microSkill: How much with a cost noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses much to ask about an uncountable payment amount.
audit.levelReason: A basic monthly housing-cost question is an adult beginner context.
audit.similarityNote: Uncountable amount question, not the number of emails.

items.setupText: Choose the words that match the situation.
items.taskText: Four people want tea. We have only three cups. We ___.
items.explanation: 'Enough' means as many as needed. Three cups are not enough for four people.

rationales.have no cups: There are three cups, so the number is not zero.
rationales.have four cups: The sentence says there are three cups, not four.
rationales.have enough cups: One cup per person needs four cups; three is too few.
rationales.do not have enough cups: 'Enough' means as many as needed. Three cups are not enough for four people.

findings: The water-for-lunch item repeated its frame and ended with the vague at the front.
audit.microSkill: Not enough for a simple need
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects enough to a concrete required quantity.
audit.levelReason: Small numbers and tea cups make the sufficiency decision accessible.
audit.similarityNote: Quantity compared with need, rather than an exact-number naming task.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that presents a small amount as available and useful.
items.taskText: There is ___ milk left, so you can have some in your coffee.
items.explanation: 'A little' means a small amount and draws attention to what is available.

rationales.little: Little emphasizes how small the supply is; the requested meaning emphasizes that some is available.
rationales.a little: 'A little' means a small amount and draws attention to what is available.
rationales.a few: 'A few' goes with plural countable things, such as 'cartons', not 'milk' here.
rationales.no: No milk would leave none to put in the coffee.

findings: The original put milk in a library with an evening-course tail and gave only generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Positive a little with a mass noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes an available small amount from emphasis on scarcity.
audit.levelReason: Coffee and leftover milk make the small-amount contrast concrete.
audit.similarityNote: Tests the speaker's positive framing of a small uncountable amount.

items.setupText: Choose a grammatical expression for a number of people, without giving an exact number.
items.taskText: ___ neighbors helped us carry the sofa upstairs.
items.explanation: 'Several' indicates a number of people without specifying exactly how many.

rationales.Three: Three is grammatical, but it states an exact number, which the task excludes.
rationales.Much: 'Much' cannot go before the plural countable noun 'neighbors'.
rationales.Several: 'Several' indicates a number of people without specifying exactly how many.

findings: Students finishing a form was a repeated frame, with a/an as redundant singular foils.
audit.microSkill: Several as an indefinite number
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts a nonexact quantity with a cardinal number.
audit.levelReason: Moving furniture supplies an everyday cooperative activity.
audit.similarityNote: Indefinite count quantity in a completed action, not a stock there-are sentence.

items.setupText: Choose the form that completes this instruction in standard written English.
items.taskText: Please bring ___ ID card to the housing office.
items.explanation: Your goes before ID card to show that the card belongs to the person being addressed.

rationales.you: 'You' names the person directly; it does not show whose ID card to bring.
rationales.yours: Yours can stand alone, as in Bring yours, but cannot introduce ID card.
rationales.yourself: 'Yourself' refers to you as a person, not to a possession before a noun.
rationales.your: Your goes before ID card to show that the card belongs to the person being addressed.

findings: The original key and options were sound, but an amount-word explanation misdescribed possessive your and all wrong feedback was generic.
audit.microSkill: Your versus independent and personal pronouns
audit.pedagogicalValue: Explains the difference between bring your card and bring yours.
audit.levelReason: A practical administrative instruction suits elementary adult use.
audit.similarityNote: Retains the one useful original ID-card context; its three duplicates are replaced.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that describes the shortage.
items.taskText: Twelve guests need seats, but the room has eight chairs. There are ___.
items.explanation: 'Not enough' means fewer than needed; eight chairs cannot seat twelve guests.

rationales.not enough chairs: 'Not enough' means fewer than needed; eight chairs cannot seat twelve guests.
rationales.too many chairs: 'Too many' means more than needed; here the room needs four more.
rationales.no chairs: There are eight chairs, so saying no chairs would be inaccurate.
rationales.enough chairs: Enough would provide a seat for every guest, but four guests lack seats.

findings: The original tested enough against mostly malformed noun combinations without explaining sufficiency.
audit.microSkill: Identifying a countable shortage
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts insufficient, excessive and zero quantities in a practical plan.
audit.levelReason: A simple seating problem requires one clear comparison.
audit.similarityNote: Uses there are plus a shortage phrase and contrasts excess with insufficiency.

items.setupText: Choose the word for one more cup; no particular cup is meant.
items.taskText: This cup is dirty. Could I have ___ cup, please?
items.explanation: 'Another' means one more or a different one, without identifying a particular cup.

rationales.the other: The other identifies a particular remaining cup in a known pair; no such pair is given.
rationales.another: 'Another' means one more or a different one, without identifying a particular cup.
rationales.other: Before singular 'cup', use 'another' or a phrase such as 'the other', not 'other' alone.
rationales.others: 'Others' stands for plural things and does not go directly before 'cup'.

findings: Seeing another teacher lacked a context for another and used an unrelated phone-call tail.
audit.microSkill: Another for an unspecified replacement
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a new replacement from the remaining member of a known pair.
audit.levelReason: A cafe request makes the additional-item meaning accessible.
audit.similarityNote: Indefinite replacement; the two-lifts item later supplies a definite pair.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that emphasizes having a small number available.
items.taskText: I know ___ people in this town, so I have someone to ask for help.
items.explanation: 'A few' means a small number and presents those contacts as available.

rationales.few: Few emphasizes the smallness of the number, rather than the positive availability requested here.
rationales.a little: 'A little' describes an uncountable amount; 'people' is plural and countable.
rationales.a few: 'A few' means a small number and presents those contacts as available.
rationales.no: No people would not support having someone local to ask.

findings: Milk in a museum during a travel lesson was an artificial repetition of the A2 milk frame.
audit.microSkill: A few for a useful small number
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects positive quantity framing to a practical consequence.
audit.levelReason: Local contacts and asking for help are familiar elementary themes.
audit.similarityNote: Positive small count quantity, contrasted with the earlier uncountable milk amount.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: My partner and I work from home. ___ use the same desk at different times.
items.explanation: Both of us refers to the two speakers together and uses us after of.

rationales.Both we: Before the pronoun 'us', use 'both of us'; 'both we' does not work here.
rationales.Both of we: 'Of' takes the object form 'us', not the subject form 'we'.
rationales.Both us: Use 'We both' or 'Both of us' as the subject, not 'Both us'.
rationales.Both of us: Both of us refers to the two speakers together and uses us after of.

findings: The clinic-form sentence repeated the several-students frame with unchanged generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Both of plus an object pronoun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Builds a quantity phrase referring back to two people.
audit.levelReason: The grammar adds a short pronoun phrase to a familiar home-work context.
audit.similarityNote: Tests the form of a partitive pronoun phrase, not merely the meaning of both.

items.setupText: Choose the word that matches the two answers.
items.taskText: I asked two hotels for a room. One was full and the other was full too. ___ hotel had a room for me.
items.explanation: Neither means not one and not the other, matching the two full hotels.

rationales.Neither: Neither means not one and not the other, matching the two full hotels.
rationales.Either: Either would indicate that one or the other had a room, contrary to both replies.
rationales.Each: Each hotel had a room would say that rooms were available at both hotels.
rationales.One: 'One hotel had a room' would mean a room was available at one of them.

findings: The ID-card item repeated 1103 with only the office type changed.
audit.microSkill: Neither before a singular noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Expresses a negative result for both members of a pair.
audit.levelReason: Two simple hotel replies make the negative pair meaning explicit.
audit.similarityNote: Neither with a noun; the later either item expresses a free choice.

items.setupText: Choose the word that allows a choice of one of two days.
items.taskText: I am free on Tuesday and Thursday. You can choose ___ day for our call.
items.explanation: Either allows you to choose one or the other of the two available days.

rationales.neither: Neither would rule out both days, but both are available.
rationales.either: Either allows you to choose one or the other of the two available days.
rationales.both: 'Both' requires plural 'days' and would select two days, not one.
rationales.every: Every day extends the choice beyond the two named days.

findings: The Saturday-class chair item repeated the original sufficiency frame without a new demand.
audit.microSkill: Either as one of two available choices
audit.pedagogicalValue: Connects either with permission to select from a pair.
audit.levelReason: Arranging a call uses concrete weekdays and a single choice.
audit.similarityNote: Permission meaning for a pair, contrasted with the hotels' negative outcome.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: Please check that ___ the windows are closed before you leave.
items.explanation: All the windows includes the complete group of windows and keeps the plural form.

rationales.every: 'Every' needs a singular noun without 'the': 'every window'.
rationales.whole: 'Whole' cannot directly quantify the plural phrase 'the windows' this way.
rationales.all: All the windows includes the complete group of windows and keeps the plural form.
rationales.each: 'Each' needs a singular noun, or 'each of the windows'; 'each the windows' is incorrect.

findings: The original placed a teacher near a desk on a student portal, an incoherent appended setting.
audit.microSkill: All before the plus a plural noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes all the windows from every window and each of the windows.
audit.levelReason: A routine closing instruction tests a common determiner pattern.
audit.similarityNote: Full-group plural reference before an existing article.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that means the entire day, from morning until evening.
items.taskText: The repair took ___.
items.explanation: The whole day treats one day as a complete period.

rationales.a few hours: 'A few hours' describes only part of the stated morning-to-evening period.
rationales.every day: 'Every day' describes repetition across days, not the length of one repair.
rationales.half the day: Half the day covers only part of the full day in the task.
rationales.the whole day: The whole day treats one day as a complete period.

findings: The original milk-in-an-airport sentence had an irrelevant reminder-email tail.
audit.microSkill: Whole for one complete period
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates a whole period from recurrence and partial duration.
audit.levelReason: One repair and familiar time expressions keep the decision concrete.
audit.similarityNote: Completeness of a singular period, contrasting with all the plural windows.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase meaning more than half, without stating the exact number.
items.taskText: Eight of the ten team members cycle to work. ___ cycle to work.
items.explanation: 'Most of them' means more than half of this known group, matching eight out of ten.

rationales.Most of them: 'Most of them' means more than half of this known group, matching eight out of ten.
rationales.Half of them: Half of ten is five; eight is more than half.
rationales.All of them: All would include ten people, but two do not cycle.
rationales.None of them: 'None' would mean zero cyclists, contrary to the eight stated.

findings: Students finishing a payroll form reused the same several-students item and boilerplate.
audit.microSkill: Most of a known group
audit.pedagogicalValue: Relates most to a majority while distinguishing half, all and none.
audit.levelReason: A small explicit group makes majority meaning easy to follow.
audit.similarityNote: Majority expressed with a pronoun rather than a direct noun.

items.setupText: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence.
items.taskText: ___ apples in this bag are damaged.
items.explanation: Some of the apples selects an unspecified part of the identified bagful.

rationales.Some of: After 'some of', a noun group needs a word such as 'the': 'some of the apples'.
rationales.Some of the: Some of the apples selects an unspecified part of the identified bagful.

findings: The program-office ID-card item duplicated an already adequate possessive contrast.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical answer meaning zero.
items.taskText: How many spare batteries do we have? We have ___.
items.explanation: 'None' can stand alone and means zero batteries in this answer.

rationales.no: No needs a noun here: no spare batteries. It cannot complete We have by itself.
rationales.neither: Neither refers to two specified alternatives, not an unspecified stock of batteries.
rationales.none: 'None' can stand alone and means zero batteries in this answer.
rationales.any: We have any does not state zero; use We do not have any or We have none.

findings: The summer-class chair question was another unchanged enough frame.
audit.microSkill: None as a standalone quantity pronoun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Contrasts no batteries with none after the noun is omitted.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that says the amount is more than wanted.
items.taskText: This soup is very salty. I put ___ salt in it.

rationales.a little: 'A little' describes a small amount without saying it was excessive.
rationales.not enough: Not enough says more was needed, the opposite of the stated problem.
rationales.too many: 'Many' cannot quantify the uncountable noun 'salt' here.
rationales.too much: 'Too much salt' means more salt than wanted, explaining the unpleasant taste.

findings: The teacher/front-desk frame repeated earlier material with a review-quiz tail.

audit.similarityNote: Excessive uncountable amount rather than positive small-amount framing.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that says the number is more than the speaker can manage.

rationales.a few: A few gives a small number without expressing the excess required by the task.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence.

rationales.some useful advice: 'Some' can introduce uncountable 'advice', even when 'useful' comes between them.

rationales.many useful advice: 'Many' needs a plural countable noun; use 'much advice' or 'many suggestions'.

rationales.other: 'Other' goes before a plural noun to refer to additional or different members of a group.

items.setupText: Choose the possessive form used before 'luggage' in standard written English.

items.setupText: Choose the words that make a grammatical sentence.

rationales.Each of: 'Each of the volunteers' treats the members individually and takes 'has' in this sentence.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that makes a grammatical sentence.

items.setupText: Choose the word that emphasizes a disappointingly small number.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase for a general statement about adults, without referring to a previously identified group.

rationales.Most these: 'Most' cannot directly precede 'these'; use 'most of these'.
rationales.Most of: 'Most of people' is incomplete here; 'of' needs a determiner such as 'these'.
rationales.Most of this: This is singular, whereas people refers to the twenty participants.
rationales.Most of these: Most of these people selects the majority from the course participants just introduced.

items.setupText: Choose the word that emphasizes how limited the available information is.

items.setupText: Choose the word that means one member of the group, with no restriction on which one.
items.taskText: The code works on all six printers. You may use ___ printer.

rationales.neither: Neither would rule out both of two alternatives; six printers are available.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase meaning three additional days.
items.taskText: Repairing the roof will take ___.

rationales.another three days: 'Another' can come before a number plus plural noun to mean an additional amount.
rationales.every three days: 'Every three days' expresses a repeating interval rather than an extension.

findings: The new-teacher each-student item merely changed the teacher's description.
audit.microSkill: Another plus a number and plural noun
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends another beyond singular-noun use to an extra measured amount.
audit.levelReason: The learner distinguishes additional duration, total duration and repetition.
audit.similarityNote: Measured extension rather than an unspecified replacement object.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical sentence without repeating the noun.
items.taskText: Some clients prefer email; ___ prefer a phone call.
items.explanation: Others stands for other clients, allowing the plural noun to be omitted.

rationales.other: 'Other' needs a following noun here: 'other clients'.
rationales.another: 'Another' refers to one client and would take 'prefers', not 'prefer'.
rationales.the another: The and another cannot be combined in this way.
rationales.others: Others stands for other clients, allowing the plural noun to be omitted.

findings: Students at an airport signing a course form repeated the each frame without useful context.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how to avoid repeating a plural noun in a group contrast.
audit.levelReason: Parallel clauses require tracking the omitted noun and plural verb.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that means throughout this morning, up to now.
items.taskText: I have been answering customer calls ___.

audit.levelReason: The present perfect progressive supports an ongoing-duration interpretation.

None of money has been spent.

'None of the money' means zero of that amount. 'Money' is uncountable and takes 'has' here.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes no money from none of the money.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that matches this repeating pattern.

rationales.every other day: 'Every other day' means alternating days, with one day between watering days.

items.setupText: Choose the word that makes a grammatical comparison.

rationales.less: 'Less traffic' means a smaller amount of traffic; 'traffic' is uncountable in this use.

At least eight delegates may enter at once.

items.setupText: Choose the function of 'some' in this context of an unidentified caller.
items.taskText: Some consultant called while you were out, but I did not catch their name.

It offers a free choice of which consultant should call.
It introduces a particular caller whose identity is not given.
It expresses doubt about whether anyone called.

Any supplier could be substituted without changing the reference.

rationales.Any supplier could be substituted withou: 'A certain' points to a particular supplier, not an arbitrary member of the class.
rationales.Several suppliers are known to have miss: 'A certain supplier' is singular and does not make a claim about several suppliers.
rationales.The speaker has a particular supplier in: 'A certain supplier' can introduce a specific individual without identifying them to the audience.

findings: The little-room appendix-note item again tested an elementary mass noun against plural foils.
audit.microSkill: Specific but unnamed a certain
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates reference to a particular entity from certainty about a proposition.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Interprets a negative environment without an explicit not.

items.setupText: Choose the intended quantity in this emphatic expression.
items.taskText: Not a few residents opposed the redevelopment.
options: A considerable number of residents opposed it.
Only a small handful of residents opposed it.
items.answer: A considerable number of residents opposed it.
items.explanation: 'Not a few' is an emphatic, somewhat formal way to say quite a large number.

rationales.A considerable number of residents oppos: 'Not a few' is an emphatic, somewhat formal way to say quite a large number.
rationales.Only a small handful of residents oppose: The expression rejects the characterization of the number as merely a few.
A considerable number need not include the entire population.

findings: The compliance-report sufficient-evidence item was the fourth copy of the same mass/count test.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that presents twelve attendees as fewer than the writer considers satisfactory.

rationales.a mere: A mere minimizes the number, presenting twelve as disappointingly small in this context.

findings: The original none/each explanations gap still allowed both grammatical answers and added an evidence-table tail.

audit.similarityNote: Minimizing a count, contrasting with B2 no less than emphasizing a large amount.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that covers every rival and explicitly excludes our design from its own comparison set.

rationales.any other design: Any covers each rival and other explicitly excludes our design, yielding a comparison with all four alternatives.

findings: The empirical-appendix several-inconsistencies item merely dressed a basic plural-noun choice in academic wording.

items.setupText: Choose the force added by 'last' in this expression.
items.taskText: The archivist checked every last page before releasing the documents.

It limits the checking to the final page of each document.
It says the pages were checked in reverse order.
It says most pages were checked, with a few exceptions.

rationales.It limits the checking to the final page: 'Every last page' is an emphatic expression for all pages here, not a selection of document endings.
rationales.It says the pages were checked in revers: 'Last' adds emphasis to completeness, not an order of inspection.
rationales.It says most pages were checked, with a: 'Every last' strengthens the exclusion of exceptions rather than allowing them.

findings: The assessment-rubric little-room item repeated the same lower-level mass/count contrast.
audit.microSkill: Emphatic every last
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes completeness emphasis from literal final-position reference.
audit.levelReason: The learner interprets a conventional intensification beyond the literal adjective.
audit.similarityNote: Emphatic exhaustiveness in inspection rather than idiomatic confidence with every reason.

items.setupText: Choose the cautious wording that preserves both a very small upper estimate and uncertainty about whether any evidence exists.

rationales.no evidence whatsoever: This resolves the uncertainty as zero, making a stronger claim than the sources permit.
rationales.little, if any, evidence: Little limits the amount, while if any explicitly keeps zero evidence possible.
rationales.some evidence, if not much: Some evidence asserts a positive amount; if not much qualifies quantity without withdrawing that existence claim.

audit.microSkill: Calibrating little if any against existence claims
audit.pedagogicalValue: Selects cautious prose that does not manufacture evidence or claim its proven absence.
audit.levelReason: The editor must preserve separate limits on quantity and certainty across a paraphrase.
audit.similarityNote: Applied evidential editing extends the C1 interpretation of few if any.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence that states both coverage conditions explicitly.
items.taskText: Every site was inspected by at least one engineer, but there was no engineer who inspected all the sites.
options: An engineer inspected every site, but not all engineers inspected a site.
Each site had an engineer inspect it, but no engineer inspected every site.
No engineer inspected any site, although each site was assigned an engineer.
Every engineer inspected a site, but some sites were not inspected.
items.answer: Each site had an engineer inspect it, but no engineer inspected every site.
items.explanation: Each site secures complete site coverage; no engineer...every site excludes a single engineer with complete coverage.

rationales.An engineer inspected every site, but no: This introduces one engineer who covered all sites, contradicting the second condition.
rationales.Each site had an engineer inspect it, bu: Each site secures complete site coverage; no engineer...every site excludes a single engineer with complete coverage.
rationales.No engineer inspected any site, although: Assignment is not inspection, and denying all inspections contradicts the first condition.
rationales.Every engineer inspected a site, but som: This quantifies over engineers instead of ensuring site coverage, and explicitly leaves sites uninspected.

findings: Neither interpretation was merely a singular-noun form choice with an unrelated hearing tail.
audit.microSkill: Distributing existential coverage without a universal individual
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes one inspector per covered site from one inspector covering all sites.
audit.levelReason: Two interacting sets and a negated universal must survive reformulation.
audit.similarityNote: Coverage of sites by engineers with an explicit no-common-individual condition.

items.setupText: Choose the inference licensed by the sentence; do not treat total rejection as implied.
items.taskText: None of the reviewers accepted all of the report's assumptions.
options: There is one particular assumption that no reviewer accepted.
Every reviewer rejected or withheld acceptance of at least one assumption.
items.answer: Every reviewer rejected or withheld acceptance of at least one assumption.

rationales.Every reviewer rejected every assumption: None accepted all rules out complete acceptance, not partial acceptance.

rationales.Every reviewer rejected or withheld acce: For each reviewer, at least one assumption was outside the accepted set; the sentence need not identify a shared exception.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Avoids inferring either blanket rejection or a single shared rejected assumption.
audit.levelReason: The task distinguishes individual exceptions from an exception common to all reviewers.
audit.similarityNote: Adds cross-reviewer exception identity to the earlier explanation-coverage distinction.

items.setupText: Choose the edited summary that preserves the reference group and the strength of the claim.
items.taskText: Almost all of the letters that survive mention at least one supplier.
options: Nearly every supplier appears in a surviving letter.
Nearly every surviving letter mentions a supplier.
Nearly every letter about suppliers has survived.
Nearly every surviving letter mentions most suppliers.
items.answer: Nearly every surviving letter mentions a supplier.
items.explanation: Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.

rationales.Nearly every surviving letter mentions a: Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves which set is quantified and avoids turning per-letter reference into coverage of suppliers.

items.setupText: Choose the accurate assessment of the proposed edit.
items.taskText: Original: 'Every witness recognized someone in the photograph.' Proposed summary: 'There was one person in the photograph whom every witness recognized.'
options: The summary is equivalent; its opening merely makes the recognized person easier to refer to.
The summary weakens every to one and no longer includes all the witnesses.
The summary adds a shared recognized person; the original allows witnesses to recognize different people.
The summary contradicts the original, which requires a different person for each witness.
items.answer: The summary adds a shared recognized person; the original allows witnesses to recognize different people.
items.explanation: One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.

rationales.The summary is equivalent; its opening m: The new opening fixes a single person as recognized by everyone. The original can be true when witnesses recognize different people.
rationales.The summary weakens every to one and no: One counts the recognized person, not the witnesses; every witness still includes the full witness group.
rationales.The summary adds a shared recognized per: One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.
rationales.The summary contradicts the original, wh: The original allows different recognized people but does not require them; it also permits everyone to recognize the same person.

findings: The original less-discretion gap tested only basic mass comparison.
A prior scope replacement used an ordered steel comparison; for a finite shortlist its shared upper benchmark actually followed, making the criticism invalid.
audit.microSkill: Detecting a shared existential referent added to a recognition report
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes each witness recognizing someone from one person being recognized by every witness, using a non-ordered relation.
audit.levelReason: The learner evaluates the referential commitment added by a fluent summary without doing a numerical calculation.
audit.similarityNote: Editorial diagnosis uses recognition of people; an explicit two-witness counterexample verifies that the common-person inference can fail.

items.setupText: Choose the summary that preserves the exception while leaving the exceptional panelist's final position unstated.
items.taskText: All but one of the panelists declined to endorse the recommendation.
options: Only one panelist endorsed it; the others declined.
One panelist declined; the others did not state their positions.
One panelist has yet to decide; the others declined.
Only one panelist did not decline; their final position is not specified.
items.answer: Only one panelist did not decline; their final position is not specified.
items.explanation: All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.

rationales.Only one panelist did not decline; their: All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.
rationales.One panelist declined; the others did no: This makes one the size of the declining group instead of the exception to that group.
rationales.One panelist has yet to decide; the othe: Indecision is possible for the exception, but the original does not specifically establish it.

findings: The progress-report little-if-any item used unrelated count-noun foils and did not test nuanced interpretation.
audit.microSkill: Exception scope without inferring a positive or undecided stance
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps an exception to refusal distinct from both endorsement and known indecision.
audit.levelReason: A fluent summary must preserve a negative-predicate exception without filling an evidential gap.
audit.similarityNote: The refined item removes arithmetic and tests the wording of an exceptional person's status.

items.setupText: Choose the defensible comparison. Both journals use 'few' for a low proportion of their own submissions.
items.taskText: Journal A says, 'Few of our fifty submissions were accepted.' Journal B says, 'Few of our five thousand submissions were accepted.'

B must have accepted more manuscripts because it received more.
Each journal accepted at most four manuscripts.
B may have accepted more manuscripts than A, despite both using few.

rationales.B must have accepted more manuscripts be: A larger submission pool does not guarantee a larger accepted count without actual acceptance figures.
rationales.Each journal accepted at most four manus: 'Few' does not have a fixed ceiling of four, especially when it describes a proportion of thousands.
rationales.B may have accepted more manuscripts tha: A low proportion of a large pool can exceed a low proportion of a small pool in absolute count; 'few' alone does not settle the comparison.

findings: The interpretive-framework neither item could be solved by elementary singular agreement.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates vague proportional judgments from absolute counts and unsupported cross-group rankings.
audit.levelReason: The learner must preserve uncertainty while comparing quantification over sharply different reference populations.
audit.similarityNote: Cross-population interpretation of few rather than another single-sentence scarcity definition.

items.setupText: Choose a neutral rewrite that explicitly starts with each report and retains a sizeable count of objections separately for it.
items.taskText: Each report leaves not a few objections unanswered.

A considerable number of objections remain unanswered in every report.
Each report leaves most of the objections unanswered.
Some reports leave a considerable number of objections unanswered.
items.answer: Each report leaves a considerable number of objections unanswered.
items.explanation: A considerable number makes not a few direct, while keeping that quantity inside the claim made separately about each report.

findings: The dissent/none item rejected grammatical each without establishing the intended position.
audit.microSkill: Neutralizing litotes while preserving per-report quantity scope
audit.pedagogicalValue: Removes rhetorical understatement while retaining explicit per-report distribution and avoiding an added majority claim.
audit.levelReason: Register editing must preserve the size assessment, the information order and the scope of the per-report quantity.

items.setupText: Choose the rewrite that restricts the quantified group to samples collected before noon.
items.taskText: The laboratory rechecked all the samples that were collected before noon. Later samples are outside this statement's claim.

Every sample collected before noon was rechecked.
All the samples were collected before noon and were rechecked.
Every rechecked sample had been collected before noon.
items.answer: Every sample collected before noon was rechecked.
items.explanation: The collection-time modifier remains inside the group quantified by every, preserving the original restriction.

rationales.Every sample collected before noon was r: The collection-time modifier remains inside the group quantified by every, preserving the original restriction.

findings: Several untested assumptions in a memorandum was another simple noun-fit item.
audit.microSkill: Preserving a quantifier's restricted domain in a rewrite
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps a temporal restriction attached to the correct event and avoids reversing a universal claim.

audit.similarityNote: Temporal restriction and implication reversal extend B2 group-restriction reading.

items.setupText: Choose the phrase that retains the defined class and allows reporting a first instance of it.
items.taskText: A discrepancy affecting the final total must be investigated. If ___ is discovered, record it separately.

rationales.any such discrepancy: Such preserves the defined property; any allows an instance to trigger the condition without assuming an earlier instance.

audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves a previously defined class while avoiding an unsupported existence claim.
audit.levelReason: Reference, restriction and conditional uncertainty interact in a compact formal phrase.
audit.similarityNote: Class-preserving anaphora rather than an unrestricted report-any-fault condition.

items.setupText: Choose the revision that preserves both exhaustive use and the small number of sources available.
items.taskText: The historian consulted what few independent sources there were.
options: The historian consulted all the independent sources available, which were few.
The historian consulted a few of the independent sources available.
The historian consulted fewer independent sources than expected.
The historian consulted independent sources whenever any became available.
items.answer: The historian consulted all the independent sources available, which were few.
items.explanation: What few combines all of the available set with an assessment that the set was small.

rationales.The historian consulted a few of the ind: A few of selects a small subset and does not retain consultation of the full available set.
rationales.The historian consulted fewer independen: 'Fewer' introduces a comparison with an expectation, not the totality of the available small set.
rationales.The historian consulted independent sour: Whenever adds a repeated timing condition and does not state exhaustive consultation of the small set.
rationales.The historian consulted all the independ: What few combines all of the available set with an assessment that the set was small.

findings: The evaluation-report little-if-any item repeated an awkward report-about-a-lesson-plan frame with weak countability foils.
audit.microSkill: Exhaustive what few in a fused relative phrase
audit.pedagogicalValue: Preserves total coverage while retaining scarcity in an editorial paraphrase.
audit.levelReason: A compressed construction encodes both reference and quantity stance.
audit.similarityNote: Count-source exhaustive paraphrase, not the B2 mass-time phrase selection.

items.setupText: Choose the editorial objection that is justified by the original wording.
items.taskText: Original: 'Three reviewers each rejected two different proposals.' Summary: 'The reviewers rejected six distinct proposals.'
options: The summary incorrectly assumes that each reviewer rejected more than one proposal.
The summary wrongly changes rejection of a shared pair into rejection of separate pairs.
The summary assumes that the reviewers' pairs did not overlap.
The summary changes an approximate total into an exact total.
items.answer: The summary assumes that the reviewers' pairs did not overlap.
items.explanation: Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.

rationales.The summary assumes that the reviewers': Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.
rationales.The summary incorrectly assumes that eac: Two different proposals explicitly gives each reviewer more than one rejection, so that inference is licensed.
